title: Why 'Always Finish Your Antibiotics' May Not Be the Best Advice
excerpt: Growing evidence suggests that completing a full antibiotic course is not always necessary and may contribute to antimicrobial resistance — but the shift in medical guidance is proving slow.
body:
• A growing body of research challenges the long-standing advice to always finish a full course of antibiotics, with experts arguing the recommendation lacks strong evidence and may worsen drug resistance.
  • A recent U.S. survey found that 88% of adults still believe they should always complete their antibiotic prescription, even when feeling better — despite evolving clinical guidance.
  • Researchers now suggest that for many common infections, stopping antibiotics when symptoms improve may be safe and could reduce unnecessary drug exposure that fuels resistant bacteria.

For decades, doctors have dispensed a seemingly ironclad rule: always finish your antibiotics, even if you feel better. But an expanding body of medical research is challenging that conventional wisdom, suggesting the advice is not only unsupported by evidence in many cases but may actually be making the global antibiotic resistance crisis worse.

The challenge was laid out forcefully in a landmark analysis published in The BMJ by a team led by Martin Llewelyn, a professor of infectious diseases at Brighton and Sussex Medical School. The researchers argued that the "complete the course" message should be abandoned, calling it "not evidence-based and incorrect."

How the Myth Took Hold

The idea that stopping antibiotics early breeds resistant bacteria traces back to the 1940s, when Australian pharmacologist Howard Florey conducted early clinical trials on penicillin. With extremely limited supply — about four grams, barely enough for a day's treatment — early patients relapsed after treatment was cut short, and the experience became entrenched in medical doctrine.

But the biology is more nuanced than the early hypothesis suggested. A patient's body is not a petri dish with a single pathogen. It is a complex ecosystem of microbes, and prolonged antibiotic use exposes harmless commensal bacteria to the drug, giving them opportunities to develop resistance through what scientists call "collateral selection."

"We encourage policy makers, educators and doctors to stop advocating 'complete the course' when communicating with the public. Further, they should publicly and actively state that this was not evidence-based and is incorrect."

— Martin Llewelyn, Brighton and Sussex Medical School

What the Evidence Actually Shows

A 2024 viewpoint article in the Journal of Antimicrobial Chemotherapy by researchers at the University of Oxford examined the evidence gaps around symptom-based antibiotic treatment. The authors found that for most common infections, shorter courses are non-inferior to longer ones — and in some cases are associated with lower levels of resistant genes.

The researchers noted that many recommended antibiotic durations are not evidence-based and are frequently exceeded by prescribers. They proposed personalizing treatment by allowing patients to stop antibiotics when they feel better, rather than adhering to arbitrary course lengths.

For certain infections — urinary tract infections, pneumonia and sinus infections — the CDC's Arjun Srinivasan has said it is "reasonable to call your doctor and ask if you can stop your antibiotic" once fever has been absent for 24 to 48 hours and symptoms have significantly improved.

The Gap Between Science and Practice

Despite the shifting medical consensus, public belief remains firmly anchored in the old guidance. A U.S. survey published in 2026 found that 88.4% of respondents believed it is important to always finish a prescribed antibiotic course, with 76.3% reporting they had received this advice from a physician.

Only 17.5% of respondents had ever been told by a clinician to stop antibiotics when feeling better. Yet 59.2% said they would feel at least somewhat comfortable receiving such advice — suggesting the public may be more receptive to updated messaging than many clinicians assume.

Critical Exceptions

Not all infections fall into the "stop when better" category. Serious conditions affecting the heart valves, bones and bloodstream typically require full courses. Tuberculosis demands extended, strictly adhered-to treatment. The emerging guidance is not a blanket permission to abandon prescriptions — it is a call for physicians to tailor advice to the specific infection and patient.

The World Health Organization has quietly moved away from its earlier "finish your prescription" messaging, though public health communication has been slow to catch up. As antimicrobial resistance claims an estimated 1.27 million lives annually worldwide — with South Asia among the hardest-hit regions — the stakes of getting this right continue to grow.
